name: Ammolite
physical: Traditionally associated with a sense of vitality
Crystal healers link it to a surge of energy
Many people wear it as a morale-lifting piece
summary: Ammolite is a rainbow-coloured gem from fossilised ammonite shell in Alberta, Canada, prized for vitality, creativity and abundance in crystal tradition.
intro: Ammolite is one of the rarest gems of the modern age, cut from the iridescent shell of fossilised ammonites found in the Bearpaw Formation of southern Alberta. Under the right pressure and mineralisation, the original nacre of the shell preserved its structure, and its microscopic layers diffract light into brilliant reds, greens, oranges and, rarely, blues and violets. The colours flash and shift like a miniature aurora. Because the layer is thin, pieces are usually stabilised as doublets or triplets with a backing and a clear quartz or glass cap. Fine ammolite is ranked among the rare organic gems, and it is the official gemstone of Alberta.
history: The Blackfoot people of the Alberta region, known as the Siksika, have long valued the shining fossil under the name iniskim, or buffalo stone. According to tradition, the stones helped call bison to the hunt, and they were kept as sacred talismans. Commercial mining and cutting began in the 1960s and 1970s, and ammolite was recognised as a gem by the World Jewellery Confederation in 1981. A Canadian company opened mines in the 1980s, and the stone gained fame as an opulent jewellery material. Ammolite is sometimes called korite after a mining company, and calcentine for its calcite-rich composition. Production remains small and carefully managed.
meaning: Ammolite is regarded as a stone of vitality, creativity and abundance, carrying the glowing energy of ancient seas. Practitioners link it to the Solar Plexus, Heart and Crown, saying it supports confidence, joyful expression and a sense of connection to nature's long history. In the Blackfoot tradition, it is the stone of the buffalo and of provision, and some use it as a symbol of prosperity. Its flashing colours are read as a sign of inspiration and imagination, and artists and makers often keep it nearby. Because it is a fossil, it holds a theme of life continuing in new forms. These associations are traditional and not medical claims.
howToUse: Wear ammolite as a pendant or ring to bring colour and confidence to your day; set in protective bezels, it will last well. Hold a piece in sunlight and watch the colours shift as a mindfulness exercise. Place it on a desk or creative workspace to spark ideas. Display a specimen on an altar to honour the sea that formed it. In a grid, use it as a centre stone for a creativity or abundance intention. Handle with care, as the thin iridescent layer can wear away.
care: Ammolite is soft and often layered, so protect it from knocks, heat, chemicals and prolonged sunlight, which can fade or crack the layers. Wipe with a soft, slightly damp cloth, never soak or use ultrasonic cleaners. Cleanse with sound, smoke or moonlight, and avoid salt. Store apart from harder gems in a soft pouch. Remove jewellery before washing, swimming or exercising. Do not expose it to sudden temperature changes.
identify: Genuine ammolite shows vivid colours that change with angle and typically appears as a thin layer on a dark or grey backing, often with a quartz or spinel cap. Look for natural crack-like patterns, called dragon-skin. Imitations include dyed fossil shell, resin, foil-backed glass and doublets sold as solid. Real stones are expensive; low-priced pieces are likely treated or reconstructed. Ask for the source, ideally Alberta, and whether the piece is a doublet or triplet.

faq.a: Ammolite is the fossilised, iridescent shell layer of ammonites, found mainly in Alberta, Canada. Its microscopic structure produces flashing reds, greens and oranges, and it is cut into gem cabochons.
Only a small area of Alberta produces gem-quality material, the colour layer is thin and fragile, and cutting is demanding. Fine, bright, large pieces are rare, so prices rise sharply for top grades.

faq.q: How do I care for ammolite jewellery?
faq.a: Keep it away from knocks, heat, chemicals and long sunlight. Wipe with a soft slightly damp cloth, dry it and store it in a pouch. Avoid soaking or ultrasonic cleaners.
